one_liner: SurrealDB's pure-Rust async LSM key-value engine with OCC transactions; vendor benchmark shows ~3x RocksDB fsync'd write throughput.
what_it_does: SurrealKV is SurrealDB's embedded, versioned key-value store. It is an LSM tree with snapshot-isolated optimistic transactions, savepoints, forward and reverse range iteration, optional time-travel reads (set_at, get_at, history) and encryption at rest with online key rotation. The API is its own Rust crate: TreeBuilder builds a Tree, and a Transaction offers set, get, delete, range and an async commit(). It is not the RocksDB API, though a bundled pure-Rust reader can import existing RocksDB BlockBasedTable v2-v7 data. The same engine targets Linux, macOS, Windows, and browser WebAssembly over OPFS.
how_it_is_fast: Writes use a group-commit pipeline modeled on Pebble's. Each committing transaction claims a slot in a 1024-slot lock-free MPSC ring with one atomic fetch_add, checks for conflicts against recent commits (Bloom-filter-assisted), and publishes the slot. A single background flusher drains every contiguous ready slot, writes them as one WAL append with one fsync, applies them to the arena-skiplist memtable, and advances the visible sequence number. Because commit() is an awaitable future, far more transactions than worker threads can share one fsync. In contrast, crud-bench's RocksDB adapter calls RocksDB's blocking commit() directly inside async tasks, which probably limits how many commits RocksDB can group per fsync at 48 workers; that is our reading of the adapter code, not a measured cause. Reads are lock-free MVCC snapshot lookups through the memtables and then leveled SSTables (64 KB prefix-compressed blocks, 10-bit/key Bloom filters, sharded block cache), and large values can move to a WiscKey-style value log.
when_to_use: Rust services on Tokio with many concurrent small transactions that each need fsync-before-ack durability. This is where group commit pays off: 105K synced creates/s at 128 clients vs RocksDB's 31.8K in the vendor run.
You need multi-key snapshot-isolation transactions with savepoints, or built-in versioned/time-travel reads (with_versioning, get_at, history), without layering MVCC on top of a plain KV store.
One storage engine must also run in the browser: wasm32-unknown-unknown in a Web Worker, persisting to OPFS, with a migrator for existing IndexedDB stores.
You want a Rust-native build and don't want to compile librocksdb-sys. Remaining native code is small C codecs such as zstd.
Point-read-heavy workloads whose working set fits in memtable plus block cache. The vendor run shows 1.60M reads/s on a 50K-key dataset.
when_not_to_use: Range-scan-dominated workloads: in the same table LMDB (27,446 ops/s) and libmdbx (16,005) beat SurrealKV's 8,361 scans/s. An mmap B+tree is the better fit.

Tight RAM budgets. Peak memory was 1.35 GB vs RocksDB's 393 MB in the vendor run. Issue #397 measured compactions needing 16-22 GiB, with an OOM restart loop on a ~16 GB store; the fix merged on 2026-09-25 is not in any crates.io release yet.

Datasets much larger than RAM or long-running write-heavy stores. The only published benchmark uses 50K keys, which fit in memory. Compaction is leveled-only, and a maintainer agreed in issue #309 that leveled is a poor fit for versioned data.
Code that needs the RocksDB API or ecosystem: C/C++ callers, RocksDB-specific tuning, or features the README does not document, such as column families or merge operators.

Anything that needs a settled, well-tested release. It is 0.x, and the benchmarked 'V2' engine is 120 commits past the latest crates.io release (0.21.4). 2026 fixed several correctness bugs: broken first-committer-wins (#376), no fsync after compaction (#390), UB in the memtable arena (#393) and range-iterator boundary defects (#395). One anecdotal HN report (June 2026, older version) also found SQLite 15-60x faster per op for a single client.

integration.dependencies: tokio (runtime required), affinitypool, arenaskiplist, byteslice, quick_cache, parking_lot, bytes, snap, zstd, lz4_flex, crc32fast, xxhash-rust, aes-gcm, chacha20poly1305, chacha20, blake3, subtle, tracing, async-trait, rand. Also rustix on Unix, windows-sys on Windows, wasm-bindgen/web-sys/getrandom on wasm. Three in-workspace migration crates (RocksDB, SurrealKV v1 and IndexedDB readers) are always compiled in.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.86 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, edition 2021), plus a Tokio runtime.
integration.platforms: README lists Linux x86-64/aarch64, macOS x86-64/aarch64, Windows x86-64, and wasm32-unknown-unknown (browser Web Workers with OPFS). CI also builds Apple and Android targets. The README's claim of io_uring on Linux does not match main, where WAL and SSTable I/O use the affinitypool thread pool on every platform.
integration.thread_safety: One Tree is shared across tasks (crud-bench shares it through an Arc across 128 clients). Each Transaction belongs to one task. Concurrency control is optimistic, first-committer-wins, with snapshot isolation (not serializable).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — not API-compatible with RocksDB (Rust-only Tree/Transaction API with async commit). It can import existing RocksDB BlockBasedTable v2-v7 data on startup or with `skv migrate`, but only as a one-way migration.

gotchas: Default durability is Durability::Eventual, which writes to the OS page cache without fsync. The benchmark figures use Durability::Immediate, set per transaction. Set it yourself if you need the durability the benchmark measured.

Needs Tokio. build() spawns background tasks with tokio::spawn and commit() is async. Call tree.close().await before exit: Drop only schedules an async close when a runtime is current, and otherwise just logs a warning.

A commit that loses a write-write conflict returns TransactionWriteConflict and closes the transaction, so retry with a new transaction. Isolation is snapshot, so write skew is possible, and get_for_update does not stop it between transactions that only read a key.

The benchmark config differs from the defaults. crud-bench turns on the value log (off by default), sets a 256 MB memtable (default 100 MB) and sizes the block cache in GB (default 32 MB). docs/ARCHITECTURE.md is marked WIP and still describes the older mutex-based commit path (src/commit.rs and src/oracle.rs no longer exist on main).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Badger when you are in Rust/Tokio or need browser OPFS support; both offer WiscKey value separation and snapshot-isolated transactions, but Badger is Go. Pick Speedb, ToplingDB or PsiTri instead when you need the RocksDB API as a drop-in or a C++ consumer, since SurrealKV only offers its own Rust API and a one-way RocksDB data import.
verified_claims_summary: On SurrealDB's own crud-bench harness (Threadripper 9970X, 128 GB DDR5, PCIe 4.0 NVMe, bare metal; 50K keys, 48 Tokio workers, 128 clients, --sync), SurrealKV reached 105,072 creates/s vs 31,777 for RocksDB (SurrealDB's surrealdb-rocksdb 0.24.0-surreal.5 fork, as an OptimisticTransactionDB), a 3.31x gap. It also reached 1.60M vs 693K point reads/s (2.31x) and 8,361 vs 2,406 scans/s (3.47x). The Rust toolchain is not stated; crud-bench's release profile uses LTO, opt-level 3 and codegen-units 1. README git history shows the SurrealKV row re-measured at least three times on 2026-09-24/25 (point reads 901K -> 1.18M -> 1.60M, creates 88K -> 105K), while RocksDB's create and scan figures never changed. The build measured is unreleased main, while crud-bench main pins surrealkv 0.21.2.
status_note: Very active: 120 commits since v0.21.4 (2026-08-26), most of the V2 engine landed 2026-09-24..26, and the memtable was swapped on 2026-09-26. It is Apache-2.0, has 555 stars and ~1.06M crates.io downloads (mostly via SurrealDB), but it is pre-1.0 and the benchmarked code is not on crates.io yet, so pin a git revision or wait for the next release.
